title: Love God, Serve Man -- Ch. 8: Why is the Catholic Church in Politics?
keywords: Why is the Catholic Church in Politics?

primary_topics: Chapter 8 of 'Love God, Serve Man' -- CJP's comprehensive answer, as PPCRV national vice chairman and chief legal counsel, to the question why the Catholic Church is getting involved in politics, organized as the WHY, the WHAT and the HOW of the Parish Pastoral Council For Responsible Voting.

The theology of Church involvement: Vatican II's doctrine of integral development and its redefinition of 'church' to include the laity, PCP II's call for lay participation in political affairs with competence and integrity, and three CBCP pastoral letters on the 1992 elections.

The definition and structure of the PPCRV as a national, parish-based, political but non-partisan lay movement supported by the hierarchy, accredited by the Comelec as its national citizen's arm and aiming at 2.3 million members in 2,300 parishes across 78 dioceses.

The defense against the charge of violating the separation of Church and State, and the claim that a 2.3 million-strong non-partisan movement could be the stabilizing force -- 'the rock upon which the state may build its foundation' -- should a plurality-elected presidency be contested.
sub_topics: The questions put to him at the outset -- why the Church is getting involved in dirty politics, whether it wants to be smeared by its mud, and whether this violates the separation of Church and State -- and his three-part plan of answer (WHY, WHAT, HOW).

The historical arc: Church involvement was largely unheard of before 1965, but during the 1986 snap election and peaceful revolution the CBCP under Ricardo Cardinal Vidal issued its 'Joint Pastoral Exhortation on the Snap Election' and then condemned the poll's fraud as 'unparalleled.'

The escalation for 1992: whereas in 1986 the CBCP merely endorsed the civic organization NAMFREL, now the Church directly sponsors the PPCRV, born of the confluence of Vatican II, PCP II and three recent CBCP pastoral letters.

Vatican II (1962-1965): the need for man's total or integral development, Christianity as liberation in the present life and not merely salvation for the next, the redefinition of 'church' to include the laity, the laity's equality with the clergy in dignity and mission with no need of a mandate beyond baptism, and Christifideles Laici's charge that the lay faithful are never to relinquish participation in public life.

PCP II (January 20 - February 17, 1991): its theological direction that, politics having become an obstacle to integral development, the lay faithful must participate more actively with singular competence and integrity; and Resolution 28, giving the laity the twin duties of forming the civic conscience and promoting the election of leaders of true integrity, while bishops, priests and religious must refrain from partisan politics and from using the pulpit for partisan purposes.

The three CBCP pastoral letters: the July 22, 1991 letter naming three indispensable requirements -- a wise, informed and formed electorate that rejects payoffs, patronage and personalities; conditions enabling free choice free of guns, goons and gold; and organization down to the precinct level against ballot-box stuffing, switching and the intimidation and bribery of election officials.

The PPCRV's answering slogans: rejection of the three Ps in favor of principles, platforms and performance with unceasing prayer, rejection of the three Gs in favor of 'the glory, grace and gospel of God,' and a pledge to poll-watch and organize parishes down to the precinct.

The second and third letters: 'Renewing the Political Order' of November 28, 1991, with its Maka-Diyos, Maka-Tao and Maka-Bayan standard answered by the PPCRV's 'Qualification Standards for Candidates for Public Service'; and the January 31, 1992 letter identifying the manipulative use of money, not violence, as the major danger, which is harder to fight because giver and receiver do not announce their unholy transactions.

The WHAT: his lawyer's comprehensive definition of the PPCRV, unpacked part by part -- national (2,300 parishes, 78 dioceses, at least 2.3 million members), parish-based and therefore the only mass-based electoral movement reaching directly into the precincts, political but non-partisan (members who campaign or announce their choices are considered resigned), lay-led, and hierarchy-supported through a five-man Board of Advisers with two cardinals as honorary co-chairmen.
The Comelec's unanimous en banc resolution of February 18, 1992 accrediting the PPCRV as its national citizen's arm.

The objectives: the immediate one of educating voters in the responsible use of the vote guided by conscience, the ultimate one of the common welfare, good government and democracy, an educational thrust of five seminar modules, secondary poll-watching and assistance to groups like Media Quick Count, and special emphasis on the youth, since 60 percent of voters are below age 30.

The HOW at national level: a trimedia campaign with P10 million in donated air time and print space from PLDT, San Miguel and Meralco; the Qualification Standards' guidelines for disqualification and qualification, asking what a candidate is, what he stands for and what he has done; a Research Committee on national candidates; and publications including Bacani's 'Church in Politics,' Msgr. Bayani Valenzuela's 'Katesismo Sa Pagboto,' the 'Ten Commandments of Voting' and the 'Voter's Prayer.'

The question whether a Catholic may vote for a non-Catholic, answered with a clear yes provided the candidate practises his faith, supported by Bishop Bacani's observation that no non-Catholic aspirant has proclaimed a position the Church could not live with.

Parish-level activities: educational and candidates' fora, distribution of materials, sign-up campaigns, prayer and fasting rallies, legal, education and research committees, and practical counsel to vote early, prepare a list beforehand and poll-watch.

The conclusion: the PPCRV as a permanent triennial movement and a 'faith response,' the three reasons it does not violate the separation of Church and State, the observation that clergy who ran would not be violating the Constitution though PCP II calls it divisive, and the warning that with eight presidential candidates and a likely plurality winner of perhaps 30 percent, a fraud-tainted election could rock the country with discontent, strife and instability.

stances.claim: The Church belongs in political life because Vatican II's doctrine of integral development requires a Christian to act out his faith in every sphere -- including the polling place and public office -- so that the Church must be wherever there is sinfulness, persecution, injustice and violation of human dignity.
stances.rhetorical_move: argument from magisterial authority: Vatican II, Christifideles Laici and PCP II marshalled in sequence to convert a political question into a theological one

stances.claim: The PPCRV does not violate the separation of Church and State, for three reasons: it is led by and composed of lay people though priests and bishops advise, it is non-partisan and endorses no candidate or party, and no constitutional provision or statute is violated by lay people forming non-partisan electoral movements even with clergy as advisers.
stances.rhetorical_move: three-point legal rebuttal delivered in counsel's voice, enumerated and answered in order

stances.claim: The manipulative use of money is the major danger of the 1992 election -- harder to fight than guns and goons because the giver and the receiver do not announce their unholy transactions, and a monstrous temptation in a country where most voters are poor.
stances.rhetorical_move: adopting the CBCP's third pastoral letter and sharpening it with the asymmetry between visible violence and invisible bribery

stances.claim: Even if men of the cloth were to run for public office they would not be violating the Constitution, though the PPCRV does not encourage it because PCP II holds it would be divisive of the flock they shepherd.
stances.rhetorical_move: separating the legal question from the pastoral one, and yielding on prudence while holding the legal ground

notable_anecdotes: The opening challenge: he voices the objections in his readers' own words -- 'Politics is dirty. Does the Church want to be smeared by its mud?' -- before answering them.

The answering chants: he recounts the PPCRV's thunderous 'YES' to the bishops' three requirements, rejecting the three Ps for principles, platforms and performance, the three Gs for 'the glory, grace and gospel of God,' and promising to pray unceasingly.
The lawyer's definition: he pauses to define the PPCRV 'comprehensively, as a lawyer would,' then dissects his own single-sentence definition clause by clause.

The non-Catholic candidate question: he reports the question often asked at his fora and answers it with a clear yes, requiring only that a Christian live gospel values and a Muslim follow the Koran faithfully, backed by Bishop Bacani's book.

The closing scenario: he imagines a president elected by as little as 30 percent of a field of eight, a fraud-tainted count, refusals to concede, and the PPCRV's 2.3 million members standing as the moderating force before, during and after the elections.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 8 of 'Love God, Serve Man' reprints the article Atty. Artemio V. Panganiban, national vice chairman and chief legal counsel of the Parish Pastoral Council For Responsible Voting, published on the front page of the Philippine Daily Inquirer on March 11, 1992 as a summary of speeches he had delivered around the country. He opens with the objections he kept hearing -- politics is dirty, the Church will be smeared by its mud, and involvement violates the separation of Church and State -- and answers them under three heads: why the PPCRV was organized, what it is, and how it will achieve its goals. Church involvement, he explains, was largely unheard of before 1965, but grew through the 1986 snap election, when the CBCP under Ricardo Cardinal Vidal exhorted the faithful and then condemned the poll's unparalleled fraud; for 1992 the Church moved from endorsing NAMFREL to directly sponsoring the PPCRV, a step he traces to three sources. Vatican II taught man's total or integral development, redefined 'church' to include the laity, recognized the laity's equality with the clergy in dignity and mission, and through Christifideles Laici charged the lay faithful never to relinquish participation in public life. PCP II directed that, politics having become an obstacle to integral development, the laity must participate with competence and integrity, while its Resolution 28 barred bishops, priests and religious from partisan politics. Three CBCP pastoral letters then demanded a formed electorate rejecting payoffs, patronage and personalities, conditions free of guns, goons and gold, and organization down to the precinct -- to which the PPCRV answered with principles, platforms and performance, with 'the glory, grace and gospel of God,' and with a pledge to poll-watch. Defining the movement as a lawyer would, he describes it as a national, parish-based, political but non-partisan lay movement supported by the hierarchy, covering 2,300 parishes in 78 dioceses with a projected 2.3 million members, accredited by the Comelec on February 18, 1992 as its national citizen's arm, devoted to voter education through five seminar modules with special emphasis on the youth, and running a trimedia campaign, Qualification Standards, a research committee and parish-level fora. He concludes that the PPCRV cannot be violating the separation of Church and State because it is lay-led, non-partisan and forbidden by no law, and that with eight presidential candidates and a likely plurality winner, its members could be the rock upon which the state may build its foundation.
